title: Royal Nepal raised about $7,400 on Labor Day, sends $6,150 to Nepal flood relief - The Alexandria Brief
description: Royal Nepal raised about $7,400 on Labor Day, sends $6,150 to Nepal flood relief  The Alexandria Brief
publisher.title: The Alexandria Brief
full_article:
ALEXANDRIA, Va. - Royal Nepal Restaurant collected about $7,435 during the Labor Day fundraiser it held for flood relief in Nepal and has sent $6,150 to the Nepal Relief Fund, the restaurant said in a video posted Thursday.

The difference between the two figures reflects taxes and other necessary deductions, the restaurant said. It posted a screenshot confirming the transfer.

The Mount Vernon Avenue restaurant, which is normally closed Mondays, opened Sept. 7 and pledged the day's entire sales to relief efforts through the Nepal government's official channels. Its staff volunteered their time.

The restaurant had set a $5,000 goal. In a video posted Wednesday, it thanked everyone who came, donated, volunteered or shared the appeal, and said the day had exceeded that target. Photos and video the restaurant shared from Sept. 7 show a full dining room, with every table occupied.

"The fundraiser was truly successful, and we are so grateful to every single person who came, donated, volunteered, shared the message, and stood with Nepal during this difficult time," the restaurant said.

In Thursday's post, the restaurant said it hopes the money reaches people in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, among the districts hardest hit, and provides safety, shelter and support. It said it hopes government relief organizations will continue to show how the funds are being used to help affected families.

The scale of what they were raising for

The flash floods late last month destroyed roughly 7,500 homes in Nepal and left another 20,000 needing repair, according to the Associated Press, which reported that at least 12 hydropower projects were damaged. More than 1,300 people had been reported dead in Nepal and Tibet as of this week, with about 5,000 still missing.

Nepal's disaster authorities put preliminary damage at $2.56 billion, close to a fifth of the country's roughly $14 billion annual budget, the AP reported. Some estimates of the full rebuilding cost run to $4 billion or $5 billion. The disaster is an early test for a government that took office in March after a year of political upheaval, and Nepal has asked for international help.

Against that, $6,150 from a restaurant on Mount Vernon Avenue is a small sum. It is also a full day's work from a staff that gave it away.

Royal Nepal said it would keep posting updates on the transfer and on how the money is being spent.

The restaurant is at 3807 Mount Vernon Ave.

Patel is a recent graduate of the school’s Adult Reconstructive Fellowship. The university said he traveled to Nepal with his wife, Akanksha Patel, his mother, Shilpa Patel and his father-in-law, Umeshkumar Patel on a pilgrimage after his graduation.

According the post, Patel and his family were likely at their hotel when the catastrophic flooding happened. The hotel was reportedly swept away by the floodwaters and they are currently declared missing.

title: Vigil honors those affected by Nepal disasters - sdsucollegian.com
description: Vigil honors those affected by Nepal disasters  sdsucollegian.com
publisher.title: sdsucollegian.com
full_article:
Shisir Roka is an SDSU biotech major from Nepal. One morning, he woke up, and like usual checked his phone for messages or mail that he might have missed. Instead, he saw headlines breaking the news of the deadly floods in his home country.

“My sleep just vanished in instance,” Roka said when recounting that morning. “I got news early in the morning, but it was already late evening in Nepal. So, I got stressed if my family was OK or not because a whole day was passed already back in Nepal.”

He was able to call his parents and found out that they were OK. Back in Nepal, not everybody can say the same.

According to an article from the Associated Press, the flood killed more than 1,300 people and left 5,000 missing. It was caused by a glacial collapse that wiped out settlements, roads and bridges in its path.

In response, the Nepalese Students’ Association (NeSA) held a candlelight vigil to honor the lives lost and affected by these floods.

Attendees gathered on the Sylvan Green, where Vice President of NeSA, Prasidika Adhikari, spoke about the flood and introduced the club adviser and other faculty to come speak.

Shelly Bayer, senior director of student engagement, said around 70 people showed up to the event.

Roka was one of the students attending the vigil. He said that when he saw videos of the flood across social media he couldn’t believe what he was seeing.

“I thought it was straight out of movie or like AI videos, but it was not. So it was really hard to see,” Roka said. “And then like, I’m here in the United States and my families are back there.”

Samitinjaya Dhakal, an assistant professor and adviser for NeSA, said that disasters like this are especially hard on international students since it’s difficult for them to just go home.

“It’s the helplessness that the students might feel in situation like this,” said Dhakal. “They are thousands of miles away from their hometown… there’s nothing that they feel like they can do about it. They cannot go back and come here because it takes weeks for them to go and come here as well, and takes thousands of dollars.”

Junior nursing major Shreya Paudel said when she first heard about the flood, she could only think of wanting to be back in Nepal.

“The first and very important thing is, like, you want to be present there. Be with your family, be with your people be with your country,” Paudel said. “But you can’t and that’s the most heartbreaking thing.”

Paudel also said that it was difficult being able to concentrate on personal things, and could not be mentally present when she knew what her home country was going through.

“It’s impacting every one of us,” Paudel said.

Among the uncertainty, Roka said that Nepalese and other international students should support each other during hard times.

title: Indiana Nepali community unites raises funds for victims of flood - Purdue Exponent

For the Nepali community of Greater Lafayette, it was uniquely hard to see the effects of the August floods in northern Nepal.

Many are from Nepal or have family still in the country — even without being personally affected, people like Sadhana Chhetri and Rojina Thapa said they wanted to be able to do something to help those who were affected.

“We're representing a small nation, but big things are happening there, and that needs worldwide support,” president of the Nepali Society at Purdue Chhetri said.

As executive officers with NepSAP, they saw the damage caused by the disaster and wanted to help however they could from halfway across the world.

“The entire community, especially on the northern side of Nepal, have been completely devastated,” Thapa said. “It's very disheartening to see how innocent lives have been changed within a couple of minutes.”

With only a week of planning, NepSAP organized a fundraiser with the help of community businesses like Momo And Beyond and Thai Essence. All of the money raised from the event will be donated directly to the Nepal prime minister’s disaster relief fund to help in recovery efforts.

Members of the Greater Lafayette community were invited to join the club and its community partners for a meal of Nepali food for a suggested donation of $20, followed by a candlelight vigil to remember those who lost their lives to the disaster.

“I know we can't compensate for that loss. But as an international community, we can at least give a hope, a real hope,” Thapa said.

Amidst the grief and concern borne of the floods, the Nepali community around Purdue said the presence of others from their home helped to create a safe place and pull everyone together to help create positive change.

Attendees of the Nepali flood-relief fundraiser hold candles in a moment of silence for the people who died in the floods. Amelia Angelone | City Editor

“It feels like a family,” said Saroj Baral, a member of the Purdue Nepali community. “Just to come together and share this feeling and try to contribute as much as possible.”

Chhetri says they were happy to welcome everyone regardless of background to Wednesday’s event, saying it’s important to spread awareness and action to those outside of the Nepali community.

While the fundraiser was quickly organized to meet the need for donations for recovery efforts, Chhetri says even a small donation from someone in Indiana is still an important part of helping to fund disaster relief in Nepal.

“The disaster won't just be over just because the floodwater has gone. We need continued support because the recovery for those communities will take a while,” Chhetri said.

The flag of Nepal sits surrounded by candles after the fundraiser and vigil Wednesday night. Amelia Angelone | City Editor

As the Greater Lafayette community learns about what is affecting the people of Nepal through NepSAP, Thapa says she hopes people see the reality of climate change in the disaster. She says the floods came as a result of unusual glacier melt as a result of warming climate and gave the people of Nepal little to no warning of the incoming disaster.

“This is a reminder that climate change is actually happening,” Thapa said. “People who are contributing less to climate change are actually paying a heavier price because of its consequences.”

title: DNA main hope for identity, but backlog overwhelms Nepal forensic labs - The Times of India
description: DNA main hope for identity, but backlog overwhelms Nepal forensic labs  The Times of India
publisher.title: The Times of India
full_article:
Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.



Nepal's forensic laboratories are in a race against time 15 days after the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli flood, with thousands of DNA samples arriving at facilities accustomed to processing fewer than 900 tests in an entire year. As visual identification becomesdifficult because of decomposition and mutilation, DNA is now the main hope of putting names to 1,265 unidentified bodies and human remains.The latest count shows 2,678 DNA samples have been collected for identification - 1,286 from the dead and 1,412 from relatives. Nepal Police's forensic laboratory alone has received 1,240 samples for DNA and related examinations, including 808 blood samples from relatives, 348 teeth and bone samples from the dead and 84 fingerprint samples. Blood samples for profiling have arrived from 26 districts. "Samples from the deceased and their relatives are continuously being received. We are working day and night," laboratory chief SSP Yog Bahadur Pal said.The scale of the wider disaster keeps the pressure mounting. Nepal has recovered 1,367 bodies and human remains, including 498 partial remains. Only 102 have been identified and handed over to families, while 5,132 people remain officially missing, including around 589 foreigners.Nepal has two main DNA facilities - Central Forensic Science Laboratory and National Forensic Science Laboratory. Before the disaster, the latter handled around 40-45 DNA tests a month, roughly 350 a year, while Nepal Police records show 358 DNA samples were processed over seven months in one recent fiscal year. The current influx is several times that routine annual workload."The bodies are difficult to identify because they have been badly damaged and dismembered," Nepal Police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle told TOI. "In some cases, two, even three, different families have even claimed the same body."Foreign forensic teams from India, China, Singapore and South Korea are assisting, but experts say Nepal must mobilise its own unused capacity.A parallel effort is under way using facial-comparison technology to narrow possible identities while families wait for DNA results. FaceTagr, deployed through a Nepal-specific missing-person portal, compares photographs of missing people with images of unidentified victims and reduces thousands of possibilities to a handful of likely matches for human review.Samir Panthi, founder of US-based Nowtrkit, said about 500 missing people had been registered and the system had helped generate possible matches for around 90 bodies. Panthi said facial matching worked far better with living people than with bodies affected by swelling, injury, decomposition or closed eyes.

title: Nebraska scientists link Nepal flood to climate change - WOWT
description: Nebraska scientists link Nepal flood to climate change  WOWT
publisher.title: WOWT
full_article:
OMAHA, Neb. (WOWT) - Two weeks after flooding in Nepal, CNN reports thousands of people are still missing. People in Omaha with loved ones in the country said they want more discussion about what they believe caused the disaster.

Sandeep Sharma, a University of Nebraska-Lincoln Ph.D. student, spent his early childhood in Nuwakot, a town nine miles from the flood scene.

“I still cannot, like, grasp the magnitude of what actually happened. Because nothing like that has ever happened in that region before, not to that magnitude,” Sharma said.

Sharma said he knew the roads that are now rubble. He believes the flood would not have happened without something causing it.

“I wouldn’t say, like, it’s because of climate change alone, but I would definitely say that’s been contributing, right?” Sharma said.

Scientists describe factors behind the flood

We spoke to Nebraska scientists abut these concerns, and the responses are similar.

“We know that the climate has changed naturally in the past. No climate scientist will ever tell you that the climate hasn’t changed naturally in the past. The changes that we’re seeing now, especially over the last century, with the rapid rate of increase in temperature that we’ve seen over the last 10, 20, 50, 100 years, is unprecedented from past climates,” Dr. Daniel Vecellio said.

Vecellio said long-term climate changes in the region have broken down permafrost and glacial melt, which he described as two essentials that serve as the glue holding ice and land together in regions such as the Himalayas.

Dr. Sarah Elizabeth Scales, assistant professor of epidemiology at the University of Nebraska Medical Center, agreed with Vecellio. She said the flash flood came from a piece of ice falling off a mountain, creating a landslide that turned into an inland tsunami.

“Mass movement of rock doesn’t necessarily intuitively sound like something that would be climate-related. But when you have glaciers melting and you have kind of changes in topography related to warming temperatures and changes in snowpack and glacial density, then that changes how rocks move. And so climate change very much contributed to the circumstances that allowed a landslide or a rock movement to have this level of impact,” Scales said.

Scientists say Omaha faces similar impacts

Scales and Vecellio say the people of Omaha are also feeling impacts of the changing environment.

“We’re starting to see more days of extreme heat now as global average temperatures start to increase,” Vecellio said.

“The whole concept of climate change, whether it be melting glaciers and thawing permafrost in Nepal or extreme heat here in Omaha, it’s all interconnected, because the globe continues to warm,” Vecellio said.

Scientists said the threat of climate change remains the same regardless of distance from a disaster.

“I don’t think you necessarily notice that those things are climate related until it really does come to your backyard,” Vecellio said.

For more ways to help those impacted by the flash floods, you can find resources posted by the Nebraska Nepalese Society on their website.

title: In the aftermath of Nepal's natural disaster - www.christiandaily.com
description: In the aftermath of Nepal's natural disaster  www.christiandaily.com
publisher.title: www.christiandaily.com
full_article:
Rescuers and residents make their way across heavy mud following flash floods on August 27, 2026 in Trishuli, Nepal. A sudden flood swept through the Bhote Koshi River basin in northern Rasuwa on August 26, damaging settlements, roads, and energy infrastructure as rescue teams searched for residents and foreign travelers reported out of contact. Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

My heart breaks when I read the news in the papers and media narrating the story of August 26th in Nepal. I am deeply grieved by what happened on that day. Lives were lost. Fathers and mothers lost their children, children lost their parents, and parents lost their own aging parents. Schoolchildren remain missing, and survivors are traumatized by the shock. Hundreds are injured. Entire homes have vanished. The scale of the loss cannot be captured in words.

Water in the Trishuli reportedly rose as much as nine meters in just thirty minutes, tearing through settlements across a 72-kilometer stretch.

On the morning of August 26, a glacier collapse near Langtang in the Himalayas triggered a massive ice-rock avalanche that thundered down the Lhende Khola–Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river system on the Nepal-Tibet border. Water in the Trishuli reportedly rose as much as nine meters in just thirty minutes, tearing through settlements across a 72-kilometer stretch and devastating the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading.

Bodies were carried as far as 240 kilometers downstream into India.

As at early September, over a thousand deaths have been confirmed in Nepal, with thousands more still listed as missing, and hundreds injured. Bodies were carried as far as 240 kilometers downstream into India. Tunnels at hydropower sites became makeshift shelters and death traps alike, with rescue teams still working to reach those trapped inside.

Distributing... aid to the people who actually need it has proven difficult.

What troubles me is not only the disaster itself, but what has followed it. The government took charge of the rescue operation, yet was slow and, in the crucial early hours, reluctant to let neighboring nations join the effort when every hour mattered most. Relief has been collected, and continues to be collected, yet distributing that aid to the people who actually need it has proven difficult.

Many NGOs and international agencies are asking for help. However, I have watched something painful unfold alongside the genuine generosity: a kind of competition on social media over who can be seen reaching the affected areas first.

Not relief but torture—a dehumanizing of the victims.

Too often, the people arriving on the actual site are not truly helping but creating confusions among people, sharing their pictures on social media. Imagine being a flood survivor and having one visitor after another ask you to recount your suffering, over and over, for the camera. That is not relief but torture—a dehumanizing of the victims.

This does more harm than good. Why have we lost our sense of humanity in the midst of humanitarian work? What is needed is for individuals and agencies to step in together where the government has fallen short, rather than working in isolation, each trying to attach their own name and reputation to the story of their generosity.

The government of Nepal has, at times, seemed more eager to advocate on the global stage about climate justice than to do the hard, humble work on the ground.

Where is our thinking about the future, about how people will actually rebuild their lives? Instead, we have spent our energy debating whose fault this is. Who is responsible for glacier melt in the Himalayas? There may be real truth worth examining in that question, but that conversation belongs in the right forum, at the right time. It is not the conversation for a moment when people in Trishuli and Rasuwa need food and clean water today. It is telling that the government of Nepal has, at times, seemed more eager to advocate on the global stage about climate justice than to do the hard, humble work on the ground.

Another side of this story is how Christian NGOs and churches have projected themselves in the social media, and not always wisely. Even mainstream Christian NGOs appear competitive in displaying their staff, their rescue vehicles, and their relief materials in the social media. What message do we want to convey to the world, and especially to the victims on the ground, when one person's tragedy becomes another's viral moment?

When I look at Christian NGOs and churches my grief deepens further.

When I look at Christian NGOs and churches my grief deepens further. I have seen leaders posting images of victims—some of whom have never spent meaningful time among rural communities, having lived comfortably in Kathmandu their whole lives.

Now I see their vehicles and their sunglasses at flood-affected sites, curated for the camera. They can reach a global audience and raise support quickly. But too often, the affected people become little more than material for sustaining an organization's image and funding.

There are those who quietly and genuinely serve people in need.

I want to be careful here that I am not speaking in general terms. There are those who quietly and genuinely serve people in need, and one will not notice them on social media. Their work is real, and it deserves honor even in its invisibility.

I sometimes wonder why Christian NGOs show less urgency in sharing the good news than they do in a high-urgency situation like this one. Perhaps the sustainability of the NGO, and fear of the government matters more to them than the sustainability of the people themselves.

Why do we hesitate to name the urgency of sharing the gospel?

Far less have we heard anyone speak of the urgency of eternity, and of the good news that people desperately need in moments exactly like this one. Why do we hesitate to name the urgency of sharing the gospel? Why do we not see how deeply the good news is needed, not only for temporal bodies only, but for their eternal being? How many of us see the present event as end times when the world interprets it as climate change and climate justice?

May the Lord give us eyes to see this moment rightly—to serve without seeking to be seen, to set aside our arguments about blame for the catastrophe until people have bread and shelter, and to remember that the hour is short and the harvest is great. May we be found faithful stewards of both bread for our stomachs and the Bread of Life for our souls via the gospel in the days ahead.

title: S. Korea sends 2nd disaster relief team to Nepal for flood recovery efforts - Yonhap News Agency
description: S. Korea sends 2nd disaster relief team to Nepal for flood recovery efforts  Yonhap News Agency
publisher.title: Yonhap News Agency
full_article:
SEOUL, Sept. 11 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's second overseas emergency relief team departed for Nepal on Friday to support reconstruction and recovery efforts following last month's devastating floods, the foreign ministry said.

The eight-member Korea Disaster Relief Team (KDRT) departed aboard a KC-330 military transport aircraft at 2:55 a.m. and was to arrive at Kathmandu at around 9 a.m. (local time), according to the ministry.

The aircraft also carried about 4 tons of relief supplies worth 180 million won (US$134,200), including tents, blankets and clothing. The supplies were donated by South Korean companies and other entities.

The second contingent will focus on reconstruction and recovery efforts during its seven-day mission, the ministry said.

The team consists of officials from the foreign ministry, the National Fire Agency, the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) and the National Medical Center.



Members of South Korea's second overseas emergency relief team (KDRT) depart for Nepal aboard a KC-330 military transport aircraft carrying relief supplies on Sept. 11, 2026, in this photo provided by the foreign ministry. (PHOTO NOT FOR SALE) (Yonhap)

The first 44-member KDRT contingent, dispatched to Nepal on Sept. 2 for a 10-day search-and-rescue mission, is scheduled to return home on Saturday morning.

Nine South Koreans -- six employees of Doosan Enerbility Co. and three of Korea South-East Power Co. -- went missing on Aug. 26 after massive floods and landslides hit Rasuwa District near the Nepal-Tibet border while they were working at a hydropower plant construction site.

Nepal has shifted its focus from search and rescue to reconstruction and recovery, while the Seoul government has said it will continue supporting search efforts for the missing Koreans in cooperation with Nepalese authorities and corporate rescue teams.

A government joint rapid response team that was dispatched to Nepal shortly after the floods will be reorganized into a seven-member team to support recovery and other efforts, the ministry said.

The team includes police and forensic officials, who will work with their Nepalese counterparts at a forensic science laboratory to assist in identifying victims, among other duties.

As of Thursday, more than 1,400 people had been killed and over 5,600 remained missing in Nepal and China's Tibet Autonomous Region following the disaster, according to foreign media reports.

title: Nepal calls for stronger monitoring of microorganisms due to glacier melt - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal calls for stronger monitoring of microorganisms due to glacier melt  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, a Kathmandu Post column author called for stronger surveillance of microorganisms in Himalayan glaciers and river basins due to melting ice. Glaciers may preserve bacteria, fungal spores, parasite eggs, and viral particles that entered the ice thousands of years ago.

On August 26, flooding in Bhotekoshi became the second major glacial flood in Nepal over the past 14 months. In early July 2025, the outburst of a supraglacial lake in China’s Gyirong County destroyed the Nepal-China Friendship Bridge, claimed several lives, disrupted critical infrastructure, and halted an important trans-Himalayan trade route for several weeks.

Ancient genetic material in ice

In 2021, researchers discovered viral genetic material nearly 15,000 years old in the Guliya ice cap on the Tibetan Plateau. Most of the identified genomes had no matches in existing databases. Further research traced viral communities back 41,000 years and described 1,700 viral species.

As an example of the dangers associated with thawing permafrost, the publication cites the 2016 anthrax outbreak on Russia’s Yamal Peninsula. After intense heat, the remains of infected animals thawed, and viable bacterial spores entered the environment. More than 2,300 reindeer died, dozens of people were infected, and one person died.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Antibiotic resistance genes

Researchers have also found plasmids and transposons in permafrost and Himalayan glaciers — mobile genetic elements containing antibiotic resistance and virulence genes. In samples of 30,000-year-old Siberian permafrost, scientists identified a functional vancomycin resistance gene structurally identical to variants currently circulating in intensive care units around the world.

The article says that a 2025 report by Lanzhou University considered glaciers, rivers, and lakes as an interconnected system through which resistance genes can be transported and altered downstream. The column’s author proposes that Nepal conduct metagenomic monitoring and environmental DNA analysis in glaciers and river catchments, as well as develop genetic sequencing capabilities.

According to ICIMOD’s 2023 assessment, ice loss rates in the Hindu Kush-Himalaya region in the 2010s were 65% higher than in the previous decade. The Yala Glacier in Nepal’s Rasuwa District has lost 66% of its surface area since 1974.

full_article:
Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA-10) gathered with other community leaders and members of the county’s Nepalese population Thursday night to hold a vigil for at least five Loudoun residents missing in Nepal following devastating flooding on Aug. 26.

A Tragedy Hitting Home

“It is a tragedy that has happened thousands of miles away but has really hit home for so many of us in our community,” Subramanyam told the crowd gathered at the South Riding Town Green Sept. 10. “I know many, if not almost all of you, knew someone including people in our own community who are missing right now.”

There are approximately 70 Americans that are still unaccounted for ,including 11 Virginians, according to Subramanyam. An estimated 1,300 people were killed in the floods and another 5,000 are missing.

Loudoun community gathers take a moment of silence for the thousands of people - including at least five Loudoun residents - impacted by devastating flooding in Nepal during a vigil Sept. 10, 2026. Hanna Pampaloni/Loudoun Now

“I have a couple of friends that are still missing, so it's extremely personal to me,” Sen. Kannan Srinivasan (D-32) said. “For the Nepali community and Indian American community in Virginia, this is not a strategy that's happening far away. These are our loved ones. These are our family, our friends, and our neighbors. And the pain of this tragedy runs deep to all of us.”

Family members of the five missing Loudoun residents were among those gathered Wednesday night.

“Anitha Radhakrishnan was my sister-in-law,” Anu Shankar said.

Radhakrishnan moved to the area in 2004 and was described by Shankar as “an integral part of the community.”

“She was a vibrant personality,” he said.

Shankar said Radhakrishnan was not the only member of her family reported missing after the floods.

“She was surrounded by you know loving family and friends,” he said. “We lost an entire family. It's not just her, but her sister, her sister's husband, her husband's brother, and the brother's wife. So, entire families have been wiped out, with the kids and the sole spouse left in order to pick up the parts.”

The four other known missing Loudoun residents are Anil Goel, Srinivas Sudhir Rangu, Suhindra Yapalparvi and Laxminath Gopisetty.

Subramanyam said that the community members were on a spiritual pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a sacred mountain at the Nepal and Tibet border for the Hindu and Buddhist faiths.

“What’s even more tragic is that this was, for many of them, a spiritual trip, to one of the most important and holiest parts of the world and to see this unfold is especially tragic,” Subramanyam said.

Left: Sreedhar Nagireddi holds a photo of Laxminath Gopisetty, a Loudoun resident missing after flood in Nepal killed over 1,300 people and left another 5,000 missing. Right: Community members gathered Sept. 10, 2026 to hold a vigil for those impacted by the flooding. Hanna Pampaloni/Loudoun Now

Community members led prayers for all those impacted by the flooding.

“The light that were in those souls that we lost will never go out,” Del. JJ Singh (D-26) said. “The light that we hold in our hands symbolizes the divine and the triumph of light over evil, and I'm grateful to all of you for being here, for holding you close in their memory. I'm grateful for the congressman for convening this, and I'm grateful for our faith leaders who will be speaking later and giving us more guidance. God bless the memory of those we lost, their families, and all of you.”

Unanswered Questions

Community members said they’re frustrated with the lack of information they’ve been getting about their missing loved ones.

“The families are waiting for the answers,” Sreedhar Nagireddi said.

Technology to find the missing individuals is available, he said.

“Why are families are still waiting? Why can't we find them? We have the technology. Everybody is wearing the gadgets. So why are things are waiting? … These are the things, tonight need to be answered. We need to fight for this justice for everybody, whatever that is,” Nagireddi said.

PKP Tenderhearts Foundation Founder Prabha Bhattarai Deeja said she hears those frustrations often from the region’s Nepalese community. PKP is a nonprofit whose goal is to serve the Nepalese-American community in the greater Washington, DC, metropolitan area. Currently, an estimated 30,000 Nepalese Americans live in the region, she said.

“Basically, right now there is no connection. We don't have an answer,” she said.

Often, the community feels as if the door is being shut in their face, Bhattarai Deeja said. Her goal is help find information and streamline it to the community, so they don’t lose hope. Some families have already traveled to Nepal and Bhattarai Deeja said she is able to help coordinate those trips and communication with leaders in the area.

“Subramanyam said his office is running into a variety of challenges as he works for information.

“It's challenging because you're talking about Nepal, which isn't always the most organized when it comes to record keeping, and is overwhelmed by needing to lead a very difficult rescue. And then you're also talking about China, who's an adversary who's not always been transparent with us, and so the combination makes it more difficult,” he said.

Subramanyam said local leaders are working with him to push the State Department and Department of Defense to get more advanced technology on the ground in Nepal to aid with the rescue efforts.

Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA-10) gathered community members in South Riding on Sept. 10, 2026 to hold a vigil for families impacted by flooding in Nepal. Hanna Pampaloni/Loudoun Now

“Now that they have equipment, we want this to be a thorough search and rescue. We want to make sure that we can, at the very least, bring closure of the families,” he said.

Looking ahead, Subramanyam said more needs to be done to prevent disasters like this from happening again.

“We've cut USAID funding in that area, as well as funding for predicting and preventing natural disasters in that region. That's going to come back to haunt us, I think, when it comes to not only this but of many other events that are happening around the world, we should have done more by investing up front in those types of programs, and instead we cut the funding for those programs,” he said.

title: South Korea sends second aid team to Nepal - UA.NEWS
description: South Korea sends second aid team to Nepal  UA.NEWS

full_article:
South Korea has sent a second emergency aid team to Nepal for recovery work following the large-scale floods and landslides that occurred in August. Eight members of the Korean Disaster Relief Team departed for Kathmandu aboard a KC-330 military transport aircraft, Korea Herald reports.

Recovery assistance

The aircraft also carried about four tonnes of humanitarian supplies worth 180 million won, or $134,200. These included tents, blankets and clothing. The aid was provided by South Korean companies and other organizations.

The second team will work in Nepal for seven days and focus on recovery and disaster response. It includes representatives of South Korea's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, National Fire Agency, Korea International Cooperation Agency and National Medical Center.

Search for missing people

The first contingent of the Korean Disaster Relief Team, comprising 44 people, arrived in Nepal on September 2 for a 10-day search-and-rescue mission. Its return to South Korea was scheduled for Saturday morning.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

After the disaster, Nepal shifted its priority from searching for people to recovery efforts. At the same time, South Korean authorities said they would continue searching for nine missing citizens together with Nepali authorities and corporate search teams.

Six employees of Doosan Enerbility Co. and three employees of Korea South-East Power Co. went missing on August 26 in Rasuwa District near Nepal's border with Tibet, where they were working on the construction of a hydropower plant. South Korea's government task force sent to Nepal after the floods will be reorganized into a seven-member team. It will include, among others, police officers and forensic specialists who will help identify victims at a Nepalese forensic laboratory.

As of Thursday, more than 1,400 people had died and over 5,600 were considered missing as a result of the disaster in Nepal and China's Tibet Autonomous Region, according to foreign media reports.

title: Nepal Flood Death Toll Rises as Aid Needs Soar - International Organization for Migration
description: Nepal Flood Death Toll Rises as Aid Needs Soar  International Organization for Migration
publisher.title: International Organization for Migration
full_article:
Kathmandu/Geneva 8 September 2026 – Humanitarian needs are growing rapidly in Nepal after devastating floods last month affected 84,000 people. The death toll has risen to 1,356 while nearly 4,900 remain missing, according to figures reported on 07 September by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA). Roads, bridges, health facilities, and schools have suffered extensive damage.

As thousands of families struggle with displacement, loss and uncertainty, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) is appealing for USD 20.5 million to assist 43,000 people in support of the Government of Nepal-led response. Aligned with the inter-agency flash appeal launched by the UN and humanitarian partners, IOM's response focuses on strengthening displacement tracking and site coordination, while scaling up shelter, health, and protection assistance for displaced and affected communities.

“For thousands of families, the immediate shock of the floods has been followed by immense uncertainty about their next steps," said Helene Fors, IOM Chief of Mission in Nepal. "Our priority is to ensure that humanitarian action is guided by reliable information and that critical assistance reaches those who need it most.”

IOM teams are already on the ground supporting the response, including in hard-to-reach locations. IOM has conducted initial assessments at holding centres where displaced families are currently residing and has provided critical medicines to health authorities. However, sustained funding is required to expand assistance to affected communities.

Priorities include emergency shelter support, particularly as winter approaches; access to health and psychosocial support services; and targeted protection support for people facing heightened risks, including women, children, older persons, and persons with disabilities.

By expanding the use of its Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), IOM is also helping authorities to track displacement locations and population movements to identify urgent needs so assistance can be directed where it is needed most. As thousands of displaced people shelter in schools, monasteries, public buildings and host communities, IOM will help ensure they can access assistance, services and protection as co-chair of the Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) Cluster, led by the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction (DUDBC).

IOM urges the international community to act now and help ensure that affected communities receive the assistance and protection they need.

title: Omaha organizations to host fundraiser for Nepal flood victims - KMTV 3 News Now Omaha
description: Omaha organizations to host fundraiser for Nepal flood victims  KMTV 3 News Now Omaha

full_article:
Devastating loss — At least 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 remain missing after floods swept along the Nepal-Tibet border last month, likely caused by a glacier collapse. Local response — The Hindu Temple of Omaha, the Nepalese Society of Nebraska, and several Indian regional organizations are hosting a community food festival fundraiser, with all donations going to the Nepal Prime Minister's Flood Relief Fund. Open to all — The event is not just for the Nepali and Indian communities — organizers say it is open to everyone in the Omaha metro area, reflecting a message that helping others transcends language, ethnicity, and nationality.

WEST OMAHA, Neb. (KMTV) —Local organizations are rallying to support victims of devastating floods in Nepal, hosting a community food festival fundraiser this Sunday at the Hindu Community Center in West Omaha.

The Hindu Temple of Omaha, the Nepalese Society of Nebraska, and several Indian regional organizations are directing all donations from the event to the Nepal Prime Minister's Flood Relief Fund.

Last month, at least 1,300 people lost their lives when heavy floods swept along the Nepal-Tibet border. According to Nepal's Disaster Management Agency, the floods were likely caused by a glacier collapse, and more than 5,000 people still remain missing.

Genandra Behndari, founder of the Nebraska Nepalese Society, said he was shocked to hear the news from his home country.

"I heard that news from Nepal and it was so devastating. I couldn't believe that could happen. No one could have thought that could happen, that kind of disaster."

Rajesh Sharma, President of the India Association of Nebraska says the event is open to everyone in the community.

"Since it impacts many countries, we want to make sure that the awareness about destruction is shared among our larger society that we have, so the event is open to all," Sharma said.

President of the Hindu Temple of Omaha Deep Kashyap said unity is at the heart of the effort.

"If we don't have unity then there is nothing. This happened due to force of nature, none of us can beat it, but this gives us an opportunity to go and show the world how much all of us can go and be together," said Kashyup.

The festival will showcase a variety of authentic Nepali and Indian foods, bringing together residents from across the Omaha metro area.

"Help doesn't have any language, it doesn't have any ethnicity, it doesn't belong to a country. When a person needs help, this is our first and foremost duty as a human being to help," said member of the Hindu Temple of Omaha, Alekha Dash.

The food festival runs from 10:30 a.m. to 2 p.m. this Sunday at the Hindu Community Center at 2445 S. 130th Circle in West Omaha.
